1.title: Measuring a Revolution
1.text:
Measuring a Revolution

A radian is one over 2 pi of a revolution, so one full revolution is 2 pi radians.

Our big question for this lesson: how would you describe the rotation of a hurricane? To get there, we need a language for spinning things.

Grab something circular, like a DVD, and mark one point on its edge. Turn it counterclockwise and watch the mark. When the mark comes back to where it started, the DVD has made one complete revolution.

How do you measure part of a revolution? The two most common ways are degrees and radians. A degree is one three-hundred-sixtieth of a revolution, the marks on a protractor. In math and physics we use the radian, which comes from the ratio of a circle's circumference to its radius. In one revolution, a point on the edge of a wheel travels 2 pi times the wheel's radius. So the radian is defined as one over 2 pi of a revolution, and one full revolution is 2 pi radians. We abbreviate radian as r a d.

2.title: Angular Displacement
2.text:
Angular Displacement

Angular displacement is the change in an object's angle as it rotates; counterclockwise is positive.

We use the Greek letter theta for the angle of rotation. Figure 1 shows several common fractions of a revolution in radians. By convention, counterclockwise rotation is positive and clockwise rotation is negative. As an object rotates, its change in angle is called its angular displacement.

Earth makes one complete revolution, 2 pi radians, in 24 hours. So in 12 hours it turns through pi radians, and in 6 hours, one fourth of a day, it turns through pi over 2 radians. In 48 hours it turns through two full revolutions, or 4 pi radians.

Seen from above the North Pole, Earth spins counterclockwise, so its rotation is positive. But look from below the South Pole and the same spin looks clockwise, so it's negative. The sign depends on your point of view!

4.title: Measuring Distance
4.text:
Measuring Distance

A point a distance r from the center that rotates through angle theta moves a distance x equals r theta.

How far does a point on a spinning object travel? A point on the edge moves 2 pi times the radius in one revolution. In general, as Figure 2 shows, a point a distance r from the center that turns through an angle theta moves a distance x equals r times theta. Here r is the point's distance from the center, theta is the angle it rotates through, and x is the distance it travels along its curved path.

If r is in meters, you might expect r times theta to come out in meter-radians. It doesn't! The radian is a dimensionless ratio of x to r, so x is simply in meters.

5.title: Angular Velocity
5.text:
Angular Velocity

Angular velocity is angular displacement divided by the time taken: omega equals delta theta over delta t.

How fast does a DVD spin? Velocity is displacement divided by time. In the same way, angular velocity is angular displacement divided by the time it takes. We use the Greek letter omega: omega equals delta theta over delta t.

Just like regular velocity, if the angular velocity changes during the time interval, this gives the average angular velocity. The instantaneous angular velocity is the slope of a graph of angular position versus time.

Angular velocity is measured in radians per second. For Earth, omega sub E equals 2 pi radians divided by 24.0 hours times 3600 seconds per hour, which is 7.27 times 10 to the negative 5 radians per second. Counterclockwise rotation gives positive angular displacement, and it gives positive angular velocity too.

testIt.how: Set the spin rate and tap the wheel to plot two seconds. ω is the slope of θ versus t.

6.title: Linear Speed and Rigid Bodies
6.text:
Linear Speed and Rigid Bodies

A point a distance r from the axis moves with linear speed v equals r omega; every part of a rigid body rotates at the same angular velocity.

If an object rotates with angular velocity omega, a point a distance r from the axis moves with linear velocity v equals r times omega. Someone standing on Earth's equator moves at v equals 6.38 times 10 to the sixth meters times 7.27 times 10 to the negative 5 radians per second, which is 464 meters per second. That's fast!

Earth is a rotating rigid body, as Figure 3 shows. Points at different latitudes travel different distances each turn, but they all rotate through the same angle. All parts of a rigid body rotate at the same rate. The Sun isn't a rigid body: different parts of it rotate at different angular velocities. Most objects in this module are rigid bodies.

7.title: Angular Acceleration
7.text:
Angular Acceleration

Angular acceleration is the change in angular velocity divided by the time taken: alpha equals delta omega over delta t.

What if the angular velocity changes? Say a car speeds up from 0.0 meters per second to 25 meters per second in 15 seconds. In those same 15 seconds, the angular velocity of its 0.64-meter-diameter wheels goes from 0.0 radians per second to 78 radians per second. The wheels have angular acceleration: the change in angular velocity divided by the time it takes. We use the Greek letter alpha: alpha equals delta omega over delta t, measured in radians per second squared.

If the change in angular velocity is positive, the angular acceleration is positive too. Defined this way, it's the average angular acceleration over the time interval. To find the instantaneous angular acceleration, take the slope of a graph of angular velocity versus time. And a point a distance r from the axis has linear acceleration a equals r times alpha.

So how do angular velocity and angular acceleration compare? Angular velocity tells you how fast the angle is changing. Angular acceleration tells you how fast the angular velocity is changing.

8.title: Linear and Angular Measures
8.text:
Linear and Angular Measures

x equals r theta, v equals r omega, and a equals r alpha link linear and angular motion.

Table 1 sums it all up. Displacement: linear x in meters, angular theta in radians, linked by x equals r theta. Velocity: linear v in meters per second, angular omega in radians per second, linked by v equals r omega. Acceleration: linear a in meters per second squared, angular alpha in radians per second squared, linked by a equals r alpha.

Notice the pattern. Each angular quantity, multiplied by the distance from the axis, gives the matching linear quantity.

9.title: Rotational Frequency
9.text:
Rotational Frequency

Rotational frequency is the number of complete revolutions per second: f equals omega over 2 pi.

The number of complete revolutions an object makes in one second is its frequency of rotation, f equals omega divided by 2 pi. Since one revolution is 2 pi radians, dividing the angular velocity by 2 pi converts radians per second into revolutions per second.

A computer hard drive is a great example. Listen closely when a computer with a spinning hard drive starts up, and you can hear it whir. Hard drive frequencies are given in revolutions per minute, or R P M. Common drives spin at 5400 or 7200 R P M, and high-performance drives at 10,000 or 15,000 R P M. The faster the drive spins, the faster it can find or store information.

So, back to our hurricane. You can describe its rotation with these same tools: its angular displacement, its angular velocity in radians per second, and its angular acceleration as it spins up or slows down. Seen from above in the Northern Hemisphere, hurricanes spin counterclockwise, so their angular velocity is positive.
